title: Twenty thousand sexes
teaches: Mating types, fused threads and the two-nucleus stage of a mushroom's life
summary: **Most mushroom fungi mate by fusing hyphae.** Two mycelia meet in the soil or wood and join; there are no eggs or sperm.
**Mating types decide who can fuse.** Two mycelia can mate only if their mating-type genes differ.
**After fusing, each cell keeps two nuclei, one from each parent.** The pair divide in step, and the fungus can live this way for years.
**The nuclei fuse only in the gills.** There they join, then divide twice to make four spores, each a new mix of the parents' genes.
**The split-gill mushroom has more than 20,000 mating types.** Two mating-type genes, each with many versions, multiply into that many combinations.
**Many types make almost every stranger a mate.** With many versions, nearly any unrelated mycelium differs, but only a quarter of siblings do, so inbreeding stays rare.
**Many fungi also make spores without mating.** These copies spread a successful fungus fast; sex mixes its genes.

blocks.text: The split-gill mushroom, *Schizophyllum commune*, is one of the most widespread fungi on Earth. It grows on dead branches and logs on every continent but Antarctica, as small, tough, fan-shaped caps a centimetre or two across, grey and furry on top. Turn one over and its gills look as if each had been slit down its edge, which gives it its name. In dry weather the split edges curl over and the cap shrivels; after rain it opens again and goes back to shedding spores.

In the 1950s and 1960s John Raper and his students at Harvard crossed thousands of split-gill strains in the laboratory, pairing them two by two to see which could mate.[^raper] What they found was not two sexes, nor three, but thousands of **mating types**: strains that can mate with each other but not with their own kind, which is the work sexes do, though they look the same. Later counts put the total at more than 23,000. Any one of them can mate with almost any unrelated strain. Why a fungus would have so many sexes begins with how it mates at all.

Mushroom fungi have no eggs and no sperm. Each spore grows into a mycelium whose cells carry one nucleus each, with a single set of the fungus's genes. When two such mycelia grow into each other in the soil or in a log, their hyphae can meet, open their walls and fuse. That is mating.

What happens next is peculiar to fungi. The two nuclei, one from each partner, do not merge. They pair up and travel together. Every cell of the new mycelium has two nuclei side by side, one from each parent, and when the cell divides they divide in step, so that each new cell again gets one of each.[^clamp] A mycelium of this kind can grow for years, and almost every mushroom you see, and the fairy ring of lesson 1, is built of two-nucleus hyphae. In effect the fungus lives most of its life as a married couple whose genes do not mix until the very end.

Not every pair can fuse and stay fused. Each mycelium carries **mating-type genes**, and two mycelia can mate only if their versions differ. In many fungi there is a single mating-type locus with just two versions. Baker's yeast, a fungus that lives as single cells, is like this: its two types are called *a* and α, and they behave like two sexes, since any *a* can mate with any α and with no other *a*.

The split-gill has two mating-type loci, A and B, and both must differ between partners.[^loci] In 1920 the German botanist Hans Kniep worked out this two-part pattern. What Raper's group added, and laid out in a book in 1966, was the number of versions of each: hundreds of versions of A and dozens of B. Every combination of an A and a B is a different mating type, which is how the count passes 20,000.

A mycelium cannot travel to find a mate. It mates with whoever happens to grow into it, and the most likely partners are its own close relatives, grown from spores of the same mushroom and landing nearby. Mating with a sibling, as in animals, tends to bring out harmful genes and makes offspring less varied.

blocks.caption: The chance that a stranger, or a sibling from the same mushroom, can mate with a given mycelium, as the number of mating-type versions grows. With one gene, partners must differ at it; with two, at both. A model where every version is equally common.
blocks.task: Raise the versions with one gene, then with two

blocks.text: With two versions of one gene, half of all strangers and half of all siblings are possible mates: no help against inbreeding, and half of all meetings wasted. Add versions and a random stranger becomes more and more likely to differ, until almost any unrelated mycelium will do. Siblings, though, only ever carry the two versions their parents had, so the share of compatible siblings stays put. With two genes it falls to a quarter. Many mating types make outbreeding nearly certain and inbreeding rare, without any need to go looking.

New versions arise now and then by mutation, a copying slip in the DNA. Rare versions have an advantage over common ones: a mycelium with a rare version can mate with almost everyone it meets, so rare versions spread. As one becomes common, more of the mycelia it meets share it, and its edge fades. Over long stretches of time this keeps adding versions and keeps them all in use, which is how the split-gill came to have so many.

The two nuclei stay apart through all of the mycelium's growth and through the building of the mushroom. They fuse only at the very end, in the cells on the surface of the gills. There each pair merges into one nucleus with two sets of genes, the only cell in the whole life in which both sets share one nucleus. Almost at once that nucleus divides twice, shuffling and halving the genes, into four new nuclei.[^meiosis] Each moves into one of four spores budding on prongs on top of the cell, and those are the spores that Buller's drop throws off.

blocks.caption: The life of a mushroom fungus. Orange and teal mark the two parents' nuclei, purple the one cell where they fuse. Not to scale.

blocks.text: So each spore carries a new combination of its parents' genes, including their mating-type versions. Spores from one mushroom fall in four mating types, and a spore has a one-in-four chance of being able to mate with a sibling picked at random, which is the sibling figure in the model.

Mating is only half the story. Most fungi can also make spores without it, by pinching off copies from the tips of hyphae. The blue-green mould on an orange or the grey fuzz on a strawberry is a carpet of copies, made in hours and in vast numbers. A copy has its parent's exact genes, which is no loss if those genes are doing well on the food at hand.

For some common moulds no one could find a sexual stage at all, and they were classed for a century as fungi that had given sex up. Careful searches keep turning it up. The blue mould used to make Roquefort cheese was shown in 2014 to have both mating types and the genes for mating, and to be capable of sex, after a century of being thought sexless. Copies spread a fungus quickly; sex, now and then, keeps its genes shuffled.

blocks.caption: Five questions on how fungi mate
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How do two mushroom-forming fungi mate?
choices: One releases sperm that swim to the other
Their spores fuse in the air
items.why: Mushroom fungi have no eggs or sperm. Two mycelia grow into each other and their hyphae fuse, if their mating types allow it.

items.ask: What is unusual about a mushroom fungus's cells after mating?
choices: Each has two separate nuclei, one from each parent
Each has no nucleus at all
Each nucleus has four sets of genes
items.why: The partners' nuclei pair up without merging and divide in step. They fuse only in the gills, just before spores are made.

items.ask: How does the split-gill reach more than 20,000 mating types?
choices: Two mating-type genes each come in many versions, and every combination is a type
Every spore makes a brand-new mating type
items.why: Hundreds of versions of one gene times dozens of the other gives tens of thousands of combinations, each a mating type.

items.ask: With many mating-type versions, what happens to the chance that two siblings can mate?
choices: It stays the same, because siblings carry only their parents' versions
It rises to nearly 100%, like strangers
items.why: Siblings share their parents' versions, so many versions in the population do not help them. With two genes, a quarter of sibling pairs can mate, while almost any stranger can.

items.ask: Where do a mushroom fungus's two nuclei finally fuse?
choices: In cells on the surface of the gills, just before spores form
In the spores, after they land
At the moment the two mycelia first meet
items.why: The two-nucleus stage lasts through the mycelium and the mushroom. The nuclei fuse in the gill cells, then divide twice into the nuclei of four spores.

raper.title: Raper's crosses
raper.text: John Raper, a mycologist at Harvard, made the split-gill one of the first fungi whose genetics was worked out in detail. His 1966 book *Genetics of Sexuality in Higher Fungi* set out the scale of the two-gene system, and the fungus is still a standard laboratory species.

clamp.title: Clamp connections
clamp.text: In many mushroom fungi, each time a two-nucleus cell divides, a small hook grows back over the new cross wall and carries one of the dividing nuclei past it. The hooks stay as little bumps beside each cross wall, called clamp connections, and a mycologist looking for them under a microscope can tell at a glance that a hypha has mated: a clamp forms only in a cell carrying both parents' nuclei.

loci.title: Two genes or four
loci.text: Strictly, each of A and B is a **locus**, a short stretch of chromosome containing two tightly linked sub-genes (Aα and Aβ, Bα and Bβ). Because partners need to differ at only one sub-gene in A and one in B to mate, each locus behaves in crosses like a single gene with hundreds or dozens of versions: about 288 for A and 81 for B, giving 23,328 mating types in all.

meiosis.title: Meiosis and the basidium
meiosis.text: This double division is **meiosis**, the same division that makes eggs and sperm in animals and pollen and ovules in plants. The club-shaped gill cell in which the two nuclei fuse and undergo meiosis is called a **basidium**, and mushroom fungi belong to the group named after it, the basidiomycetes.
